turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hi. I guess what brings me in is that I just keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put. Like, during my client interviews—I'm a private investigator, so I have to do a lot of sit-down intake meetings. Mostly corporate fraud, sometimes infidelity, though I try to avoid those now. The last cheating spouse case I took, the guy was actually just secretly going to a bird-watching group. Can you believe that? His wife was so sure, but nope, he was just really into owls. They meet at that park over on 5th, which has a completely terrible parking situation by the way, I got a ticket there last month. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll be in a client meeting and I just keep getting out of my chair. The same thing happens during these tutoring sessions I do on the side, and even at my book club. We're reading this massive historical biography right now, and Brenda—she hosts it—makes these incredible little cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off. But people are really starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen. Brenda actually pointed it out last week, asking why I kept abandoning my seat every ten minutes... so, yeah, I figured I should probably talk to someone about it.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly states that others have noticed they 'can't just sit and listen.'
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports repeatedly getting up and abandoning their seat during client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club meetings where they are expected to stay put.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have this same trouble staying in your seat when you were a child in school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. It's funny you ask that because my mother actually kept all my old grade-school report cards. She has them in this massive cedar chest at her house down in Florida—she moved to Boca a few years ago. She complains about the humidity constantly, but she absolutely dominates her local bingo league, so she refuses to leave. 

But anyway, yeah, if you look at those old report cards, every single one of them says basically the exact same thing: that I was a bright kid, but I just couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mom still jokes about it all the time. She says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. Which is kind of hilarious now, right? Given that I actually do investigate things for a living. Though, I'll tell you, real investigations are way more paperwork than pacing. I actually have to buy these specific blue gel pens in bulk for my office because the regular ballpoints just smudge everywhere when you're writing fast... wait, what was I saying? 

Right, school. Yes, I definitely had the exact same problem back then.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts during the response, going off on tangents about his mother's bingo league and blue gel pens before losing his train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly confirms that his childhood report cards noted he 'couldn't stay in my seat'.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient recalls pacing through classrooms as a child, indicating inappropriate restlessness and moving about.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient mentions that his childhood report cards also stated he couldn't 'wait my turn'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also find it difficult to sustain your attention on tasks or paperwork, leading to careless mistakes?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, paperwork is a huge part of the job, like I was saying. I actually just reorganized my whole filing system last month. I found these incredible vintage steel cabinets from a liquidation sale—well, it was an old library that was closing down, actually. They weigh an absolute ton. The movers I hired, these two college kids, they looked like they wanted to kill me when they had to get them up the stairs to my office. One of them, I think his name was Tyler, he was wearing these really flimsy canvas sneakers, which is just a terrible choice for moving heavy furniture. You really need good arch support and steel toes if you're carrying things. I learned that the hard way during a stakeout back in '98 when I had to chase a guy through a construction site. Ruined a perfectly good pair of loafers. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, careless mistakes. No, I'm actually very meticulous with my files and reports. You kind of have to be, you know? If you make a careless mistake on a surveillance log and it goes to court, the opposing counsel will just tear you apart on the stand. I saw that happen to a guy once in a deposition, it was completely brutal to watch. So, no, I don't really lose focus on that stuff. I'm pretty dialed in when it comes to the actual details and getting the facts right.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, highly detailed, and tangential response to a simple yes/no question, demonstrating excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless mistakes, stating they are meticulous and dialed in on details.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies losing focus or having difficulty sustaining attention on paperwork and tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient mentions successfully reorganizing their entire filing system, indicating a lack of difficulty with organization.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel like you are constantly 'on the go,' as if driven by a motor?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, oh my gosh, yes. It's like I have this internal engine that just won't shut off. Even on days when I don't have any field work or active surveillance, I just can't sit still. I'll go from unpacking boxes—I still have a few left from when I moved offices three months ago, which is ridiculous, I know. But I'll jump from that to reorganizing old case files, to running errands... it's like I'm constantly chasing a lead, even when there isn't one. I just have a really hard time being "off duty," you know? 

Like last Sunday, I had no cases, nothing pending. I was supposed to just relax. But by 9 AM, I had cleaned the entire kitchen, gone to the hardware store for weather stripping—which, by the way, the guy at the hardware store tried to sell me the foam kind, and I told him, "Look, foam degrades in two years, you need the rubber V-strip." He didn't know what to say to that. It's like people don't even know the products they sell anymore. Same thing happened when I was looking for a new espresso machine. The salesperson kept pushing this pod thing, and I'm like, "Do I look like someone who wants stale coffee from a little plastic cup?" I ended up buying a refurbished Italian pump machine off a guy on Craigslist. Makes incredible crema. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, being on the go. Yeah, I just never really stop moving. It's exhausting sometimes, but I just can't seem to turn it off.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by their own unrelated thoughts and stories, causing them to forget the doctor's initial question.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly states, 'I just can't sit still,' indicating feelings of restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient strongly confirms the symptom, describing an 'internal engine that just won't shut off' and stating they 'never really stop moving.'
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, rambling response filled with unnecessary details about hardware stores and espresso machines.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, drifting far off-topic into stories about weather stripping and coffee machines before realizing they lost the thread of the conversation.

turns.doctor_question: {"intent": "Assess whether the high energy and activity occur in distinct episodes or are continuous/baseline to differentiate bipolar hypomania from ADHD.", "question": "Do these periods of high energy and
turns.patient_response:
Do they happen in episodes? No, not really. It's just... it's just how I am all the time. It's like a baseline frequency I'm always vibrating at. Even when I try to take a vacation, which, let me tell you, is a nightmare. I went to this all-inclusive resort in Mexico a couple of years ago. My sister dragged me there. She's a yoga instructor, completely zen, the exact opposite of me. She can just lie on a beach chair for six hours straight and do absolutely nothing. I don't understand it. By day two, I had befriended the entire resort staff, figured out the optimal routing for the housekeeping carts, and actually helped the bartender fix the slushie machine. The motor was just jammed, it wasn't a big deal, but they were going to call a technician from Cancun who wouldn't have been there for three days. Three days without margaritas? At a resort? Unacceptable. 

Anyway, the bartender, Hector, he gave me this huge bottle of authentic mezcal to say thank you. I still have it in my pantry. I don't really drink mezcal, it's a little too smoky for me, you know? It tastes like you're drinking a campfire. I prefer a nice, crisp gin. There's this local distillery that makes one with juniper and... wait. What were we talking about? 

Oh, right, episodes. No, it's not like it comes and goes. I'm just always like this. Morning, noon, and night. It never really turns off.

symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient describes taking a vacation (a leisure activity) as a 'nightmare' and cannot understand how someone can just lie on a beach chair and do nothing.
